# Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria starts with six years of primary education, beginning around age five, culminating in a first school-leaving certificate. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) program, established in 1999, replaced earlier universal primary education efforts to provide free, compulsory, and continuous nine years of formal schooling, encompassing six years of primary and three years of junior secondary education. Subjects in primary school include Mathematics, English, Indigenous languages (Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba, Igbo), Religious Knowledge, Agriculture, Home Economics, and optional Computer Science, French, and Fine Arts. Students take a Common Entrance Examination to qualify for secondary school admission.
Secondary education is divided into three years of Junior Secondary School (JSS) and three years of Senior Secondary School (SSS), following the 6-3-3-4 system. Junior secondary covers core subjects like Mathematics, English, Social Studies, and electives including French and vocational studies. Senior secondary education includes core subjects and electives spanning sciences, social sciences, arts, and vocational courses, culminating in the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE). Secondary schools vary by sponsorship: federal government ("unity schools") which are elite and merit-based; state government schools often suffer from inadequate funding and staffing; and private/religious schools which generally offer smaller classes and better facilities at higher costs. Teacher qualifications vary by sector, with federal schools usually requiring higher credentials than state schools.
Tertiary education includes universities (federal, state, and private), polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education, with Nigeria having 153 universities as of 2017. Admission typically requires SSCE and performance on the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) exams. Education duration varies by program, e.g., 4–6 years for engineering, medicine, and law. Vocational education, overseen by the National Board for Technical Education, offers National Technical Certificates, with challenges including outdated curricula and teacher shortages. Informal education and adult literacy programs continue to play an important role but face funding and administrative challenges. Female education has improved through initiatives like UNICEF's Girls’ Education Project addressing barriers such as poverty and cultural factors, though challenges remain especially due to regional insecurity.
Overall, Nigeria’s education system has diversified offerings and ongoing reforms but faces challenges including regional disparities, teacher shortages, infrastructure deficits, and quality assurance. Efforts continue to improve literacy, digital skills, access, and equity across the country.
